items.stem: Which is a characteristic of perfect competition?
options: There are high barriers to entry
There are a few large interdependent firms
Firms are price takers selling a homogeneous product
items.answer: Firms are price takers selling a homogeneous product
items.markingKey: Many buyers and sellers, identical products, perfect information, free entry and exit.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain how a perfectly competitive industry moves from short-run supernormal profit to long-run equilibrium.
items.answer: Diagram pair: industry S and D set price P1; firm’s horizontal AR = MR at P1 above ATC at output where MC = MR, shaded supernormal profit. Free entry shifts industry supply right, price falls to P2 = min ATC; firm’s AR = MR falls until tangent to ATC at its minimum: normal profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: SR profit shown; 1 mark: entry shifts supply; 1 mark: price falls; 1 mark: LR at min ATC with normal profit [4]

items.stem: Explain why a perfectly competitive firm cannot charge a price above the market price.
items.answer: Products are homogeneous and buyers have perfect information, so if it raises its price consumers switch to identical rivals and its sales fall to zero: demand for its output is perfectly elastic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: homogeneous/perfect info; 1 mark: perfectly elastic demand [2]

items.stem: A perfectly competitive tomatoes producer sells 1000 units where price = MC = $9. At this output ATC is $10 and AVC is $6. Calculate the firm’s profit or loss.

A perfectly competitive tomatoes producer sells 200 units where price = MC = $8. At this output ATC is $10 and AVC is $6. Calculate the profit or loss and explain what the firm should do in the short run and in the long run.
items.answer: Profit = (8 − 10) × 200 = −$400; the firm should continue in the short run because P > AVC (covers some fixed costs), but leave in the long run if the loss persists.
items.markingKey: Profit = (AR − ATC) × Q [1] = −$400 [1]; compare P with AVC and ATC [1]; correct short- and long-run decision [1].

items.stem: A perfectly competitive milk producer sells 400 units where price = MC = $17. At this output ATC is $20 and AVC is $18. Calculate the profit or loss and explain what the firm should do in the short run and in the long run. Show that your recommendation minimises the loss.
items.answer: Profit = (17 − 20) × 400 = −$1,200; the firm should shut down: P < AVC so it cannot even cover variable costs. If it shuts down the loss is TFC = (ATC − AVC) × Q = −$800.
items.markingKey: Profit = (AR − ATC) × Q [1] = −$1,200 [1]; compare P with AVC and ATC [1]; correct short- and long-run decision [1]. Compare with loss on shutdown (= TFC) [1].

items.stem: Extract: The coffee shop market in Marvona is dominated by four firms with shares of 25%, 18%, 16%, 9%. Prices have remained at about $3 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio and state the market structure it suggests. (b) Using the kinked demand curve model, explain why prices may have stayed the same.
items.answer: (a) 68%; oligopoly (b) Rivals match cuts but not rises; MR has a discontinuity, so higher MC within the gap leaves price unchanged.

items.stem: Extract: The electricity supply market in Halvoria is dominated by four firms with shares of 33%, 20%, 19%, 12%. Prices have remained at about $3 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio and state the market structure it suggests. (b) Using the kinked demand curve model, explain why prices may have stayed the same.
items.answer: (a) 84%; oligopoly (b) Rivals match cuts but not rises; MR has a discontinuity, so higher MC within the gap leaves price unchanged.

items.stem: Explain why perfect competition is said to be allocatively and productively efficient in the long run.
items.answer: In LR equilibrium P = MC (allocative) and output is at the minimum point of ATC (productive), with normal profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A profit-maximising monopolist produces where
options: marginal cost equals marginal revenue, and charges the price on the demand curve at that output
items.answer: marginal cost equals marginal revenue, and charges the price on the demand curve at that output
items.markingKey: MC = MR gives Q; price read from AR at that Q.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain the profit-maximising equilibrium of a monopolist.
items.answer: Diagram: downward-sloping AR (demand) with MR below it, twice as steep; U-shaped MC and ATC. Output Qm where MC = MR; price Pm read off AR above Qm; ATC at Qm below Pm; supernormal profit = (Pm − ATC) × Qm shaded rectangle; barriers keep it in the long run.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: AR and MR; 1 mark: MC = MR output; 1 mark: price from AR; 1 mark: profit area [4]

items.stem: Explain why a natural monopoly may be better for consumers than competition.
items.answer: With huge economies of scale, one firm has lower average costs than several firms duplicating infrastructure, so price could be lower, especially if regulated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: falling LRAC across market; 1 mark: duplication avoided/lower costs [2]

items.stem: A monopolist faces demand P = 200 − 2Q (so MR = 200 − 4Q) and has constant marginal and average variable cost of $40. Calculate the profit-maximising output.
items.answer: 40 units

items.stem: A monopolist faces demand P = 50 − 0.5Q (so MR = 50 − 1Q) and has constant marginal and average variable cost of $40. Calculate the profit-maximising output, price and profit. Compare with the output and price if the industry were perfectly competitive, and calculate the deadweight welfare loss.
items.answer: Q = 10, P = $45, profit = $50; competitive Q = 20, P = $40; deadweight loss = $25.

items.stem: A monopolist faces demand P = 50 − 1Q (so MR = 50 − 2Q) and has constant marginal and average variable cost of $10 with fixed costs of $100. Calculate the profit-maximising output, price and profit. Compare with the output and price if the industry were perfectly competitive, and calculate the deadweight welfare loss.
items.answer: Q = 20, P = $30, profit = $300; competitive Q = 40, P = $10; deadweight loss = $200.

items.stem: Extract: The steel market in Zentara is dominated by four firms with shares of 31%, 23%, 15%, 12%. Prices have remained at about $3 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Using the kinked demand curve model, explain why prices may have stayed the same. (b) Explain two pieces of evidence that would suggest collusion rather than competition.
items.answer: (a) Rivals match cuts but not rises; MR has a discontinuity, so higher MC within the gap leaves price unchanged. (b) Identical price changes at the same time, stable market shares, high profits, communication between firms, prices above cost.

items.stem: Extract: The brewing market in Ostrelia is dominated by four firms with shares of 22%, 21%, 18%, 15%. Prices have remained at about $3 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Using the kinked demand curve model, explain why prices may have stayed the same. (b) Explain two pieces of evidence that would suggest collusion rather than competition.
items.answer: (a) Rivals match cuts but not rises; MR has a discontinuity, so higher MC within the gap leaves price unchanged. (b) Identical price changes at the same time, stable market shares, high profits, communication between firms, prices above cost.

items.stem: Which is a feature of monopolistic competition?
options: A single firm with high barriers to entry
Firms selling identical products as price takers
Many firms selling differentiated products with low barriers to entry
items.answer: Many firms selling differentiated products with low barriers to entry
items.markingKey: Monopolistic competition: many firms, product differentiation, free entry, some price-setting power.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain the long-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition.
items.answer: Diagram: downward-sloping AR with MR below; U-shaped ATC and MC. Output where MC = MR; at that output AR is tangent to ATC, so P = ATC and only normal profit is earned; the tangency is to the left of minimum ATC, showing excess capacity; P > MC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MC = MR; 1 mark: AR tangent to ATC; 1 mark: normal profit; 1 mark: excess capacity/P > MC [4]

items.stem: Explain why firms in monopolistic competition spend heavily on advertising and branding.
items.answer: To differentiate their products, build brand loyalty and make demand less price elastic, giving more power to set prices and shift demand to the right.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: differentiation; 1 mark: less elastic/more demand [2]

items.stem: A hair salon in Riyadh sells 400 units a week at $12 where MR = MC; average total cost is $10. Calculate its weekly supernormal profit.

A pizza restaurant in Seoul sells 500 units a week at $18 where MR = MC; average total cost is $16. (a) Calculate its supernormal profit. (b) Explain what will happen to this profit in the long run. (c) In the long run the firm sells 450 units, while minimum ATC occurs at 650 units. Explain what this shows about efficiency.
items.answer: (a) $1,000 a week (b) New pizza restaurants enter, demand for this firm shifts left and becomes more elastic until AR is tangent to ATC: normal profit. (c) Output is below the minimum-ATC output, so there is excess capacity: not productively efficient, and P > MC so not allocatively efficient.
items.markingKey: (a) (P − ATC) × Q [2]; (b) entry, demand shifts left, normal profit [2]; (c) excess capacity, productive and allocative inefficiency [2].

items.stem: Extract: The soft drinks market in Selmaria is dominated by four firms with shares of 30%, 19%, 11%, 10%. Prices have remained at about $2.5 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio and state the market structure it suggests. (b) Explain two pieces of evidence that would suggest collusion rather than competition.
items.answer: (a) 70%; oligopoly (b) Identical price changes at the same time, stable market shares, high profits, communication between firms, prices above cost.

items.stem: The key feature that distinguishes oligopoly from other market structures is
options: interdependence between a few large firms
items.answer: interdependence between a few large firms
items.markingKey: Each firm’s decisions depend on expected reactions of rivals.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain why prices may be rigid in an oligopoly according to the kinked demand curve model.
items.answer: Diagram: demand curve kinked at current price P1: elastic above (rivals ignore a rise), inelastic below (rivals match a cut). The MR curve has a vertical gap below the kink. MC can shift up or down within the gap and MC = MR still gives the same output and price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: kink and reasons; 1 mark: MR discontinuity; 1 mark: MC shifts within gap leave P unchanged [3]

items.stem: Explain why collusion may break down in an oligopoly.
items.answer: Each firm has an incentive to cheat by cutting price or raising output to gain market share; it is hard to monitor rivals; new entrants, falling demand and competition authorities also undermine agreements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: incentive to cheat; 1 mark: another reason [2]

items.stem: Two firms, Ironleaf and Cobalt Group, choose a strategy at the same time. Payoffs (profit in $m, Ironleaf first, Cobalt Group second): Ironleaf Launch new model and Cobalt Group Launch new model: (7, 9); Ironleaf Launch new model and Cobalt Group Do not launch: (20, 8); Ironleaf Do not launch and Cobalt Group Launch new model: (14, 15); Ironleaf Do not launch and Cobalt Group Do not launch: (9, 8). What is Ironleaf’s dominant strategy?
options: It depends only on its own costs
items.answer: It has no dominant strategy
items.markingKey: Compare Ironleaf’s payoffs for each choice of Cobalt Group: dominant strategy = none.

items.stem: Two firms, Delta Foods and Everline, choose a strategy at the same time. Payoffs (profit in $m, Delta Foods first, Everline second): Delta Foods Keep to the quota and Everline Keep to the quota: (11, 11); Delta Foods Keep to the quota and Everline Exceed the quota: (8, 18); Delta Foods Exceed the quota and Everline Keep to the quota: (18, 8); Delta Foods Exceed the quota and Everline Exceed the quota: (9, 9). (a) Identify any dominant strategy for each firm. (b) Identify the Nash equilibrium. (c) Explain whether the firms have an incentive to collude.
items.answer: (a) Delta Foods: Exceed the quota; Everline: Exceed the quota. (b) Delta Foods Exceed the quota, Everline Exceed the quota. (c) Joint profit is highest when Delta Foods chooses Keep to the quota and Everline chooses Exceed the quota (total $26m), which differs from the Nash equilibrium, so there is an incentive to collude, but each firm also has an incentive to cheat.
items.markingKey: (a) compare payoffs column by column and row by row [2]; (b) best response for both [1]; (c) joint-profit outcome vs Nash; incentive to cheat/prisoners’ dilemma [2].

items.stem: Extract: The airline market in Istrana is dominated by four firms with shares of 26%, 25%, 10%, 9%. Prices have remained at about $2.5 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio and state the market structure it suggests. (b) Explain two pieces of evidence that would suggest collusion rather than competition.
items.answer: (a) 70%; oligopoly (b) Identical price changes at the same time, stable market shares, high profits, communication between firms, prices above cost.

items.stem: A perfectly contestable market is one in which
options: there are no sunk costs and entry and exit are free, so the threat of entry disciplines incumbents
items.answer: there are no sunk costs and entry and exit are free, so the threat of entry disciplines incumbents
items.markingKey: Contestability depends on entry/exit costs, not the number of firms.

items.stem: Explain how contestable market theory suggests that a market with only one firm may still behave competitively.
items.answer: If entry and exit are costless, any supernormal profit would attract hit-and-run entrants, so the incumbent keeps price close to average cost (limit pricing) and is efficient.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: threat of entry; 1 mark: no sunk costs; 1 mark: normal profit/efficient outcome [3]

items.stem: Explain how price discrimination may benefit some consumers.
items.answer: Consumers in the elastic market (e.g. students, off-peak travellers) pay lower prices than under a single price, and the extra revenue may allow a service to run that would otherwise be unprofitable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower price for elastic group; 1 mark: service viable/higher output [2]

items.stem: A firm with constant marginal cost of $20 sells in two separate markets. Peak users: P = 140 − 2Q (MR = 140 − 4Q). Off-peak users: P = 40 − 0.5Q (MR = 40 − 1Q). Calculate the profit-maximising price for peak users.

A firm with constant marginal cost of $30 sells in two separate markets. Adults: P = 90 − 1Q (MR = 90 − 2Q). Students: P = 70 − 0.5Q (MR = 70 − 1Q). Calculate the profit-maximising output and price in each market and the total contribution to profit. Show which market has the less elastic demand at these prices.
items.answer: adults: Q = 30, P = $60; students: Q = 40, P = $50; contribution = $1,700. PED = P/(P − MC): 2 vs 2.5, so adults have the less elastic demand and pay the higher price.
items.markingKey: MR = MC in each market [2]; prices from AR [2]; profit = Σ(P − MC)Q = $1,700 [1]; |PED| = P/(P − MC) at MR = MC, compared [1].

items.stem: Extract: The soft drinks market in Marvona is dominated by four firms with shares of 31%, 28%, 22%, 20%. Prices have remained at about $4 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio and state the market structure it suggests. (b) Explain two pieces of evidence that would suggest collusion rather than competition.
items.answer: (a) 101%; oligopoly (b) Identical price changes at the same time, stable market shares, high profits, communication between firms, prices above cost.

items.stem: In the short run a perfectly competitive firm will shut down if price falls below
items.answer: average variable cost
items.markingKey: If P < AVC the firm cannot cover variable costs; shutting down limits the loss to TFC.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why perfect competition is said to be allocatively and productively efficient in the long run. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how a perfectly competitive industry moves from short-run supernormal profit to long-run equilibrium.
items.answer: (a) In LR equilibrium P = MC (allocative) and output is at the minimum point of ATC (productive), with normal profit. (b) Diagram pair: industry S and D set price P1; firm’s horizontal AR = MR at P1 above ATC at output where MC = MR, shaded supernormal profit. Free entry shifts industry supply right, price falls to P2 = min ATC; firm’s AR = MR falls until tangent to ATC at its minimum: normal profit.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: SR profit shown; 1 mark: entry shifts supply; 1 mark: price falls; 1 mark: LR at min ATC with normal profit [4]

items.stem: A perfectly competitive potatoes producer sells 400 units where price = MC = $10. At this output ATC is $12 and AVC is $8. Calculate the firm’s profit or loss.

A perfectly competitive tomatoes producer sells 1000 units where price = MC = $4. At this output ATC is $10 and AVC is $6. Calculate the profit or loss and explain what the firm should do in the short run and in the long run.
items.answer: Profit = (4 − 10) × 1000 = −$6,000; the firm should shut down: P < AVC so it cannot even cover variable costs.
items.markingKey: Profit = (AR − ATC) × Q [1] = −$6,000 [1]; compare P with AVC and ATC [1]; correct short- and long-run decision [1].

items.stem: Farmers in Sundara sell identical crops at prices set on a national commodity exchange. Evaluate the view that perfect competition is an unrealistic model and of little use to economists.
items.answer: Arguments for: Assumptions rarely hold, yet the model is a benchmark for efficiency; some markets (agriculture, foreign exchange) come close. Arguments against / evaluation: Useful benchmark for policy; predicts effects of entry and exit; but ignores economies of scale and innovation. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: A natural monopoly exists when
options: a firm controls a natural resource
one firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than two or more firms
the government owns the only firm
items.answer: one firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than two or more firms
items.markingKey: Economies of scale so large that LRAC falls over the whole market range, e.g. water pipes.

items.stem: Explain why a monopoly may be X-inefficient.
items.answer: Lack of competitive pressure means managers may allow costs to rise above the minimum possible for each output (organisational slack), so the firm operates above its cost curve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lack of competition; 1 mark: costs above the lowest possible [2]

items.stem: A monopolist faces demand P = 70 − 1Q (so MR = 70 − 2Q) and has constant marginal and average variable cost of $40. Calculate the profit-maximising output.
items.answer: 15 units

items.stem: Water and electricity networks in Loristan are each run by a single company. (a) Explain what is meant by a natural monopoly and why it arises. (b) ‘Natural monopolies should be owned by the state.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: One firm has lowest costs; state ownership can set P = MC or P = AC and avoid abuse. (b) Case for the view: One firm has lowest costs; state ownership can set P = MC or P = AC and avoid abuse. Case against / evaluation: Regulation of private firms (price caps) may be more efficient; government failure, X-inefficiency, political interference; investment funding. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Evaluate the view that natural monopolies should be owned by the state.
items.answer: Arguments for: One firm has lowest costs; state ownership can set P = MC or P = AC and avoid abuse. Arguments against / evaluation: Regulation of private firms (price caps) may be more efficient; government failure, X-inefficiency, political interference; investment funding. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: In long-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition, the firm’s demand curve is
options: tangent to ATC at its minimum
tangent to the average cost curve to the left of its minimum point
items.answer: tangent to the average cost curve to the left of its minimum point
items.markingKey: Entry removes supernormal profit: AR = ATC, with excess capacity.

items.stem: Explain why supernormal profits do not last in monopolistic competition.
items.answer: Low barriers to entry let new firms offer close substitutes, taking customers so each firm’s demand shifts left and becomes more elastic until P = ATC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: entry; 1 mark: demand falls until normal profit [2]

items.stem: A gym in Jakarta sells 500 units a week at $18 where MR = MC; average total cost is $13. Calculate its weekly supernormal profit.

Extract: The car manufacturing market in Dravonia is dominated by four firms with shares of 21%, 15%, 11%, 10%. Prices have remained at about $3 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Explain two pieces of evidence that would suggest collusion rather than competition. (b) Discuss whether the market is likely to be contestable.
items.answer: (a) Identical price changes at the same time, stable market shares, high profits, communication between firms, prices above cost. (b) Depends on sunk costs, brand loyalty, economies of scale and licensing; high sunk costs or regulation reduce contestability; evidence of entry/exit.

items.stem: Explain why oligopolists often compete through non-price competition.
items.answer: Price cuts are quickly matched and risk a price war that lowers everyone’s profit, so firms compete through advertising, branding, quality and loyalty schemes, which are harder to copy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price war risk; 1 mark: non-price methods [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between tacit and explicit collusion.
items.answer: Explicit collusion is a formal (usually illegal) agreement to fix prices or output; tacit collusion is coordination without agreement, e.g. price leadership.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In the shipbuilding industry of Westaria, the six largest firms have market shares of 14%, 11%, 22%, 17%, 5%, 6%; the remaining 25% is shared by many small firms. Calculate the 3-firm concentration ratio.
items.markingKey: CR3 = sum of the 3 largest shares = 22 + 17 + 14 = 53%.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain third-degree price discrimination between two markets.
items.answer: Diagram: two markets side by side with a common MC. In each market output where MR = MC; inelastic market (steeper AR) has higher price P1; elastic market (flatter AR) has lower price P2; total profit exceeds that from a single price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MR = MC in each market; 1 mark: higher price in inelastic market; 1 mark: higher profit [3]

items.stem: A firm with constant marginal cost of $30 sells in two separate markets. Business travellers: P = 70 − 1Q (MR = 70 − 2Q). Tourists: P = 110 − 1Q (MR = 110 − 2Q). Calculate the profit-maximising price for business travellers.

A firm with constant marginal cost of $10 sells in two separate markets. Business travellers: P = 130 − 2Q (MR = 130 − 4Q). Tourists: P = 40 − 0.5Q (MR = 40 − 1Q). Calculate the profit-maximising output and price in each market and the total contribution to profit. Show which market has the less elastic demand at these prices.
items.answer: business travellers: Q = 30, P = $70; tourists: Q = 30, P = $25; contribution = $2,250. PED = P/(P − MC): 1.17 vs 1.67, so business travellers have the less elastic demand and pay the higher price.
items.markingKey: MR = MC in each market [2]; prices from AR [2]; profit = Σ(P − MC)Q = $2,250 [1]; |PED| = P/(P − MC) at MR = MC, compared [1].

options: firms produce on the falling part of ATC
price equals minimum average total cost and firms earn normal profit
items.answer: price equals minimum average total cost and firms earn normal profit

items.stem: Firms in monopolistic competition have excess capacity in the long run because
options: they produce less than the output at minimum average cost
items.answer: they produce less than the output at minimum average cost
items.markingKey: Tangency on the falling part of ATC: not productively efficient.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the long-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition. (b) Explain why supernormal profits do not last in monopolistic competition.
items.answer: (a) Diagram: downward-sloping AR with MR below; U-shaped ATC and MC. Output where MC = MR; at that output AR is tangent to ATC, so P = ATC and only normal profit is earned; the tangency is to the left of minimum ATC, showing excess capacity; P > MC. (b) Low barriers to entry let new firms offer close substitutes, taking customers so each firm’s demand shifts left and becomes more elastic until P = ATC.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: MC = MR; 1 mark: AR tangent to ATC; 1 mark: normal profit; 1 mark: excess capacity/P > MC [4] (b) 1 mark: entry; 1 mark: demand falls until normal profit [2]

items.stem: A hair salon in Kuala Lumpur sells 1000 units a week at $20 where MR = MC; average total cost is $17. Calculate its weekly supernormal profit.

There are hundreds of independent cafés and restaurants in Lisbon. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the short-run and long-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition. (b) Discuss the extent to which monopolistic competition gives consumers a better outcome than perfect competition.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Variety and choice; product innovation; normal profit in LR. (b) Case for the view: Variety and choice; product innovation; normal profit in LR. Case against / evaluation: Excess capacity, P > MC, wasteful advertising; less efficient than PC; but consumers value variety. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why oligopolists often compete through non-price competition. (b) Explain why collusion may break down in an oligopoly.
items.answer: (a) Price cuts are quickly matched and risk a price war that lowers everyone’s profit, so firms compete through advertising, branding, quality and loyalty schemes, which are harder to copy. (b) Each firm has an incentive to cheat by cutting price or raising output to gain market share; it is hard to monitor rivals; new entrants, falling demand and competition authorities also undermine agreements.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: price war risk; 1 mark: non-price methods [2] (b) 1 mark: incentive to cheat; 1 mark: another reason [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain why prices may be rigid in an oligopoly according to the kinked demand curve model. (b) Explain why oligopolists often compete through non-price competition.
items.answer: (a) Diagram: demand curve kinked at current price P1: elastic above (rivals ignore a rise), inelastic below (rivals match a cut). The MR curve has a vertical gap below the kink. MC can shift up or down within the gap and MC = MR still gives the same output and price. (b) Price cuts are quickly matched and risk a price war that lowers everyone’s profit, so firms compete through advertising, branding, quality and loyalty schemes, which are harder to copy.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: kink and reasons; 1 mark: MR discontinuity; 1 mark: MC shifts within gap leave P unchanged [3] (b) 1 mark: price war risk; 1 mark: non-price methods [2]

items.stem: Two firms, Borealis plc and Everline, choose a strategy at the same time. Payoffs (profit in $m, Borealis plc first, Everline second): Borealis plc Expand capacity and Everline Expand capacity: (4, 18); Borealis plc Expand capacity and Everline Keep capacity: (13, 16); Borealis plc Keep capacity and Everline Expand capacity: (19, 7); Borealis plc Keep capacity and Everline Keep capacity: (19, 9). What is Borealis plc’s dominant strategy?
options: It depends only on its own costs
items.answer: Keep capacity
items.markingKey: Compare Borealis plc’s payoffs for each choice of Everline: dominant strategy = Keep capacity.

items.stem: Silverline, an airline in Nordavia, charges business travellers much more than leisure travellers for seats on the same flight. Explain why this is possible and profitable.
items.answer: The two groups have different PED (business demand is inelastic, leisure elastic); the airline can separate them by booking time or flexibility rules and tickets cannot be resold, so MR = MC in each market gives higher profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: different PED; 1 mark: separation/no resale; 1 mark: higher profit [3]

items.stem: A firm with constant marginal cost of $10 sells in two separate markets. Peak users: P = 30 − 1Q (MR = 30 − 2Q). Off-peak users: P = 32 − 0.5Q (MR = 32 − 1Q). Calculate the profit-maximising price for peak users.

A firm with constant marginal cost of $30 sells in two separate markets. Business travellers: P = 90 − 1Q (MR = 90 − 2Q). Tourists: P = 70 − 0.5Q (MR = 70 − 1Q). Calculate the profit-maximising output and price in each market and the total contribution to profit. Show which market has the less elastic demand at these prices.
items.answer: business travellers: Q = 30, P = $60; tourists: Q = 40, P = $50; contribution = $1,700. PED = P/(P − MC): 2 vs 2.5, so business travellers have the less elastic demand and pay the higher price.
items.markingKey: MR = MC in each market [2]; prices from AR [2]; profit = Σ(P − MC)Q = $1,700 [1]; |PED| = P/(P − MC) at MR = MC, compared [1].
